name: Bristol 450
hook: An aeroplane company built this finned racer, swept its Le Mans class two years running, then broke up all but one.
story: Bristol built aeroplanes. Big ones. So when its car division went racing, it thought like an aircraft maker. It bought a Formula Two design from ERA, a team that had just folded, and rebuilt the frame in steel tube. A Bristol six-cylinder went in the front. Just two litres. Then came the body. A teardrop canopy, and two fins sweeping back off the tail. For 1954, the gap between them was raised and filled in, after wind-tunnel work. It looked strange. It was meant to be stable. At Le Mans that June, the cars ran down the Mulsanne Straight at about 150 miles an hour. A gust burst through a gap in the trees. Other cars were thrown about. Peter Wilson's Bristol barely twitched. A small correction, and on he went. Twenty-four hours later, all three Bristols finished. Seventh, eighth and ninth overall. First, second and third in the two-litre class. Open cars did it again in 1955. Then Bristol quit racing and broke them up. Only one survives.
description: The Bristol 450 was a sports-racing car built by the car division of the Bristol Aeroplane Company at Filton. Its chassis followed ERA's G-type Formula Two car, remade in round steel tubes, with a de Dion rear axle. A 1,971 cc Bristol straight-six sat up front. The 1954 coupés wore twin rear fins, reshaped after wind-tunnel work. Three cars took the two-litre class 1-2-3 at Le Mans in 1954, and open 450s repeated it in 1955. All but one were broken up.
